# Yards First Daily | September 16, 2026

## 1. Executive read

**Most important:** OXEA has put Uber Freight in charge of day-to-day transportation across four markets and three modes. The chemical manufacturer is replacing regional management with one operating model, but neither company has explained how that model connects to physical release at its plants.

**Changed since yesterday:** A named enterprise buyer disclosed a cross-border managed-transport decision. Separately, Hitachi Energy disclosed a factory transition that could turn its existing Mississippi plant into a warehouse after production moves nearby.

**What the market is getting wrong:** A unified transportation view is not yet a unified execution process. Someone must still reconcile a changed carrier or delivery plan with equipment, documentation, and what is ready to leave the site.

**Allocation: RESEARCH.** OXEA offers a strong buyer-behavior story and a useful sales question. Hold publication until a plant-level handoff is verified.

## 2. Decision-grade signals

### 1. NEW: OXEA makes managed transportation a cross-border operating decision

**Development:** Announced September 15, OXEA selected Uber Freight to manage daily truckload, rail, and ocean transportation across the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and Europe. Chief supply chain officer Scott Farmer said OXEA wants to anticipate disruptions and respond faster as it moves beyond region-by-region management. This is the companies’ first managed-transport engagement designed from the outset to span all four markets; no operating result has been reported. [OXEA announcement](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/15/3362524/0/en/oxea-transforms-global-logistics-operations-selects-uber-freight-as-strategic-partner.html), [FreightWaves, September 15](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/oxea-taps-uber-freight-to-manage-north-american-european-logistics)

**Why now and buyer read:** OXEA has assigned a partner daily execution across modes and borders, while retaining the customer and manufacturing consequences. Chemical freight also requires specialized handling, documentation, and safety coordination. The unresolved implementation question is who can change a move when a transport plan conflicts with plant readiness.

**Yard implication: ADJACENT.** Inference, not a disclosed deployment: carrier assignments and arrival plans must eventually meet physical equipment, loading, documents, and gate release. No OXEA yard problem has been established.

**Editorial opportunity:** The useful test of a “single network” is the exception at the plant boundary, not whether headquarters has a common dashboard.

**Commercial opportunity:** OXEA plant logistics and supply-chain systems leaders; Uber Freight’s chemical managed-transport implementation team; other multi-plant chemical manufacturers changing 3PL control. **Casey’s move:** Ask both sides, “If a customer priority or carrier changes after a chemical load is prepared, who reconciles equipment, safety documents, loading status, and release authority?” Seek the named exception owner and a plant-to-carrier control map.

**Score: 26/30, A5 B3 C5 D5 E4 F4. Confidence: HIGH on the selection; MEDIUM on the physical implication.** The customer announcement establishes scope and intent, with trade corroboration. It supplies no contract value, shipment volume, site workflow, or performance baseline.

### 2. NEW: Hitachi Energy plans a factory move that may retain the old site for logistics

**Development:** Hitachi Energy announced September 15 a **$528 million** transformer factory in Gallman, Mississippi, about **6.5 miles** from its Crystal Springs plant. Construction is expected to begin late in 2026 and production in 2029. Production will then transition to Gallman; Hitachi says the Crystal Springs building will remain in use for warehousing, training, *or other* operational needs. Warehousing is a possibility, not a finalized plan. [Hitachi Energy, September 15](https://www.hitachienergy.com/news-and-events/press-releases/2026/09/hitachi-deepens-commitment-to-u-s-manufacturing-with-528-million-mississippi-transformer-factory)

**Why now and buyer read:** This is a funded network redesign, not simply another factory opening. Manufacturing, facilities, materials control, project transportation, and IT/OT must plan a production cutover while deciding what role the existing property will serve. No logistics-system purchase is disclosed.

**Yard implication: ADJACENT.** Inference: if Crystal Springs becomes storage, material identity, condition, location, and release priorities will need to survive transfers between sites. Hitachi has not published a yard design or movement volumes.

**Editorial opportunity:** A new factory can make the old one a logistics asset. The question is whether the two sites will operate as one controlled flow during the transition.

**Commercial opportunity:** Hitachi Energy’s Mississippi manufacturing operations, plant logistics, facilities-transition, and IT/OT leaders; transformer and other heavy-equipment manufacturers making nearby-site cutovers. **Casey’s move:** Ask the Gallman transition owner, “What event will change a unit’s authoritative location and release status when work moves between Crystal Springs and Gallman?” Seek the site-transition workflow owner, not a presumed YMS budget.

**Score: 24/30, A5 B3 C5 D4 E3 F4. Confidence: HIGH on the investment and transition; LOW on yard design.** Hitachi is the primary source; its alternatives for the old building and its physical workflows remain open.

## 3. Lead-story decision: DEVELOP

**Working thesis:** OXEA can consolidate transportation management across borders, but the promise becomes operational only when an exception can be resolved against what a chemical plant can safely release.

**Why Yards First has standing:** The story follows a planning change to the loading, custody, and gate decisions that determine whether freight actually moves.

**Verified anchor:** One planned operating model spans **four markets and three freight modes**. That is scope, not a measured service improvement.

**Reporting required:** Obtain one OXEA plant-to-carrier exception example; establish who owns equipment readiness, documentation, appointment changes, physical release, and the authoritative event record.

**Headline options:**

1. **A Global Freight Plan Still Has to Clear the Plant Gate**
2. **OXEA Outsourced Dispatch. Who Owns the Exc

# Yards First Daily | September 17, 2026

## 1. Executive read

**Most important:** Ferrovalle has selected an optimization layer for its Mexico City intermodal terminal while keeping its in-house terminal operating system. The design makes a useful distinction for YardFlow: recording a container’s status, deciding its best next move, and authorizing that move are related jobs, but they are not the same job.

**Changed since yesterday:** September 16 trade coverage put operating detail behind INFORM’s September 15 announcement: the planned system spans cranes, tractors, train loading, two differently controlled yards, and customs release.

**What the market is getting wrong:** Calling this “AI in the yard” misses the hard requirement. An optimized instruction must remain subordinate to the container’s current physical and legal state.

**Allocation: PUBLISH.** The signed selection and specified control boundaries support an architecture story now. Do not present a planned June 2027 go-live as an achieved result.

## 2. Decision-grade signal

### 1. CONFIRMED: Ferrovalle buys optimization around its existing TOS

**Development:** INFORM announced September 15 that Ferrovalle selected Syncrotess Optimization Plus under a contract signed in early September. September 16 reporting detailed the planned Smart Yard implementation at Ferrovalle’s Mexico City intermodal operation, which handled approximately **550,000 TEUs in 2025**. Go-live is targeted for June 2027. The initial scope covers eight rubber-tired gantry cranes, four reach stackers, and 14 terminal tractors. [INFORM announcement](https://www.inform-software.com/en/news/syncrotess/ferrovalle-and-inform-partner-to-advance-ai-powered-intermodal-operations-in-mexico-city), [Logistics Business, September 16](https://logisticsbusiness.com/it-in-logistics/ferrovalle-ai-optimisation-mexico-city/)

**Why consequential now:** This is a named operator’s contracted implementation with an explicit system boundary. INFORM will generate coordinated recommendations for storage, equipment, and train loading alongside, not in place of, Ferrovalle’s TOS.

**Enterprise buyer read:** Ferrovalle’s managing director describes a need for real-time visibility and more consistent decisions. Dispatchers currently apply substantial manual judgment to container placement, equipment, and trains. Terminal operations, TOS ownership, equipment control, customs, and implementation teams must agree which system supplies status, which recommends work, and who can override it. Ferrovalle aims to improve billable moves relative to total handling, but has reported no improvement yet.

**Yard implication: DIRECT.** The project spans a customs-cleared yard and a customs-controlled yard. Under the announced design, the TOS must confirm documentation and customs clearance before the optimizer releases a container for train loading. Crane-lift weight verification and inspection-area tractor assignments are also intended to become part of the workflow.

**Editorial opportunity:** The revealing feature is a boundary on automation: the optimizer can propose a better move, but it cannot make an uncleared container legally loadable. Report the handoff between *best move* and *permitted move*.

**Commercial opportunity:** Inland intermodal terminals, cross-border rail gateways, and multi-operator container yards with established TOS investments. Target terminal COO, intermodal operations, equipment-control manager, customs-process owner, and TOS/IT architect. **Casey’s move:** Ask an operator with an existing TOS, “When clearance or container status changes after a move is assigned, what cancels the tractor instruction, updates the plan, and proves the container was never loaded?” Seek the exception owner and the event that closes the loop, not an invitation to replace the TOS.

**Score: 28/30, A5 B5 C5 D5 E5 F3. Confidence: MEDIUM.** INFORM names the customer, contracted scope, equipment, and planned architecture and quotes Ferrovalle’s managing director. Trade coverage supplies detail, but no independent implementation result, contract value, or operator-published baseline is available.

## 3. Lead-story decision: WRITE NOW

**Working thesis:** Ferrovalle’s Smart Yard shows that automation becomes trustworthy when a recommended physical move cannot outrun the system that governs whether the cargo is allowed to move.

**Why Yards First has standing:** The decision is executed through container location, crane and tractor assignment, inspection status, customs clearance, and train loading.

**Verified anchor:** Ferrovalle’s intermodal division handled approximately **550,000 TEUs in 2025**. That is operating scale, not a claimed automation benefit.

**Additional reporting:** Confirm who can override a recommendation, how quickly changed clearance propagates to an assigned tractor, how erroneous moves are detected, and the baseline for billable versus total moves.

**Headline options:**

1. **The Best Yard Move Is Useless If the Box Cannot Legally Move**
2. **Ferrovalle Kept Its TOS. It Bought Better Decisions Around It.**
3. **An Optimizer Cannot Clear a Container Through Customs**

**Handoff for the existing Jake system (187 words):**

Ferrovalle has selected INFORM’s software for a Smart Yard project at its Mexico City intermodal operation. The division handled about 550,000 TEUs in 2025. The announced first scope includes eight yard cranes, four reach stackers, and 14 terminal tractors; go-live is planned for June 2027.

The important beat is the boundary between a suggested move and an authorized one.

Ferrovalle is keeping its internally built terminal operating system. ## 1. Executive read
